title: Firefox Can Now Block Ads on iOS (but You Have to Enable It)
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 1, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Kenneth Cheung / iStock Unreleased via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Firefox users on iOS can now get rid of a lot of ad noise when browsing on their mobile device, as Mozilla is officially rolling out native ad blocking.
                                            Most ads will be blocked, but users will still see search engine ads and sponsored content from Firefox.
                                            The feature is off by default, so you need to enable it yourself if you want to use it.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Firefox users on iOS can now get rid of a lot of ad noise when browsing on their mobile device. Following a slow "experimental" period, Mozilla is now officially rolling out native ad blocking, which you can enable once the tool is available in your app. According to Mozilla's support page detailing the new feature, Firefox's new feature can block third-party ad networks and exchanges along with many third-party ads served on websites at the network level. It can also block ad-related trackers, pop-ups, and overlays. The platform is still letting some ads through, though: For example, you'll still see ads in search results from engines like Google, Bing, and DuckDuckGo, as well as sponsored content on the Firefox Home and New Tab pages. There may also be ads that aren't covered by the EasyList filter list. Of course, Firefox isn't the only browser to natively block ads on iOS. For example, both DuckDuckGo and Brave have built-in ad blocking in their mobile apps and also allow you to disable their own search ads. Note that ad-blocking functionality doesn't extend outside of the Firefox iOS app, but URL filters in iOS 26, along with a third-party app like Wipr 2, can block ads in other apps. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Ad blocking in Firefox will be off by default. To enable it, open the iOS app, tap the three dots, and go to Settings > Browsing. Under the Content header, toggle on Ad Blocker. You can do this from the Site menu by tapping Ad Blocker (underneath the site name and URL), which will open the Browsing menu directly. The site menu will show you at a glance whether ad blocking is on or off.

            Credit: Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Microsoft Outlook is down for many users as of Monday afternoon.
                                            Downdetector highlights tens of thousands of users reports suggesting issues with Outlook.
                                            In addition, other Microsoft services, including Microsoft 365, are also down.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're trying to check your inbox or send an email in Microsoft Outlook, only to find the app uncooperative, you're not alone. Outlook is currently down for many users as of Monday afternoon. That's apparent to anyone who can't get the app to work: Downdetector, which highlights user reports for app outages, shows tens of thousands of reports as of 3:00 p.m. ET, and while the rate of reports does seem to be decreasing, thousands of reports keep coming in with every refresh.  As CNET reports, Microsoft has officially confirmed the outage itself. The company posted on its Microsoft 365 Status X account, stating: “We’ve identified an issue with an authentication component which is contributing to impact. To address this, we’ve developed a remediation strategy, and we’re applying it to a portion of infrastructure to test its efficacy. Once we’ve confirmed this resolves impact, we’ll apply the solution more broadly. For more information, please see EX1464935 in the admin center.”As such, the company should be rolling out a fix in due time, though it's difficult to say how long that may be. Recent outages have been fixed in a matter of hours, while others have stretched into the following day. At the time of writing, Downdetector shows that 38% of users are reporting issues receiving messages in Outlook, while 24% report issues with the app, and 21% with logging in. 
As it happens, Outlook isn't the only Microsoft product facing issues: Users report that Microsoft Teams, Microsoft Store, Microsoft Azur  and Microsoft 365 in general are experiencing  issues. In addition, OpenAI users are reporting issues with ChatGPT. 
            
                What do you think so far?

        Update: As of 5 p.m. EDT, the problem seems to have largely been resolved, as reports on Downdetector have dropped from a high of around 10,000 to under 500. Twitch still has not commented on the issue beyond its initial status message.If you're having some trouble logging into Twitch for a gaming session right now, it's not just you: According to Downdetector, thousands of users are reporting issues with the online gaming platform. It looks like the problems began around 2:30 p.m. EDT, when reports of access issues started to trickle in. By around 4 p.m., those numbers spiked to almost 10,000 and remain elevated as of this writing. Twitch has yet to reveal what might be causing the problem or offer a timeframe for a fix, with its status page merely sharing the following:
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Service Negatively Impacted: We have received reports of impacted services. This could manifest in chat not working, login difficulties, search impaired, etc. We're looking into the issue.No additional updates have been shared on the company's social media profiles, including X. According to Twitch, the platform experienced its last major outage two years ago, in August 2024.

title: Here's When Walmart Will Finally Start Allowing Tap to Pay
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 21, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: marekuliasz via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Walmart is finally getting Tap to Pay.
                                            The company announced the news on Friday, sharing that both Walmart and Sam's Club locations will start supporting the payment method.
                                            The rollout starts Monday, Aug. 24, at select locations, though all stores will support Tap to Pay by the end of 2026.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Any time I go to Walmart, I always forget that the store doesn't have Tap to Pay. That really shouldn't be that big of a deal, except almost every business I frequent these days does support the feature. As such, muscle memory has me pulling out my iPhone at self-checkout, only to look like a moron trying to tap to pay a NFC-free card reader. Without fail, each time I reluctantly take out my credit card and physically scan or insert it in the POS, I wonder to myself why Walmart doesn't have Tap to Pay. (I've even left my credit card stuck in the card reader, since I'm so used to not using it these days.)As it happens, those days are (thankfully) numbered. On Friday, Walmart announced that Tap to Pay is coming to its stores, as well as Sam's Club. In addition to using your credit or debit card to pay with whatever contactless method you prefer, Walmart says you'll be able to add your Walmart, Sam's Club, or OnePay cards to your digital wallet. While you can, of course, continue to pay for your items with cash, credit cards, or Walmart Pay, anyone who wants to use Tap to Pay should be able to do so without issue. It's pretty big news, even if it means Walmart is simply catching up to virtually every other store—at least the ones I typically go to. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
When is Tap to Pay coming to Walmart?According to Walmart's press release, Tap to Pay is rolling out Aug. 24 to select Walmart stores and Sam's Club locations. Starting on Monday, your local store may let you pay with your smartphone, smartwatch, contactless credit card, or any other method that supports Tap to Pay. If not, Walmart says all U.S. stores will support it by the end of this year, while all gas stations will support it by mid-2027.

            Credit: Prykhodov via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple Maps officially launched ads in search this week.
                                            You'll see ads in the new "Suggested Places" field, as well as in Apple Maps search results.
                                            You can't block Apple Maps ads, but you can choose an alternative that skips out on them completely.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        This week, Apple Maps officially launched ads in search. It's not necessarily a surprise, mind you: We learned back in October that Apple planned to roll out ads at some point. But it's still a bit jarring to see Apple actually commit to the plan. Now, most of the mainstream navigation apps come with ads, which makes getting around without dealing with ads difficult—but not impossible.How Apple Maps' ads work Once ads hit your app, you'll start seeing them when you search for new destinations. That includes both in the new "Suggested Places" section, as well as within search results as well. Like other platforms that float sponsored items to the top of search results, you'll likely want to be a bit more scrupulous, since the top pick might not actually be the most relevant to your query. What's more, there's no way to actually disable these ads. There are ad blockers for iPhone, but they're limited, and won't block Apple's own ads. As such, it just doesn't feel very "Apple" to deal with ads on the company's own navigation app—especially if you're already giving Apple money every month. While Apple Maps doesn't have a paid subscription, Apple offers plenty of services at a cost. As YouTuber Quinn Nelson notes, some users are paying $50 per month for Apple One, and still having to deal with ads on Apple Maps. Of course, it's the same story for Google Maps: Google's famous navigation app also has mandatory ads, whether you subscribe to one of Google's services or not. In Apple's view, its approach is better than competitors like Google, as the company is adamant its ads preserve your privacy. But even if that's the case, I'm not sure it's going to sell users on the new approach.
It's tough to find a good navigation alternative to Apple Maps or Google Maps. That includes Waze, which is also owned by Google and also has ads. However, there is one solid—albeit rather underground—choice for anyone whose top priority is a lack of ads.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Organic Maps is a free and open-source app that prioritizes privacy for navigation. According to the developer, the app works entirely offline, and does not track people as they use it. (How refreshing.) As such, you could download your maps, disable cellular services, and still have the ability to navigate—of course, you can use it while connected, as well. The app supports a number of features that you'll find on other more mainstream platforms, including cycling and hiking routes, turn-by-turn directions, public transit maps, and dark mode. Organic Maps uses OpenStreetMap to provide its navigation data. While the benefit of OpenStreetMap is that it's also open-source, so users all over the globe can add their own data points, it likely isn't as robust as Apple's map data, not to mention Google's decades of data. Still, users have generally positive reviews on the iOS App Store, suggesting that OpenStreetMap's data offers an adequate alternative to Apple Maps. Now, if you're used to scrolling through restaurant reviews or checking out Street View, you'll miss that here. While Organic Maps does have a search function, it's lacking compared to other platforms. This is definitely a navigation-first app, rather than a full Apple Maps or Google Maps replacement. Still, if you're looking for an ad-free alternative, there are few better options out there at this time.

title: What Is This 'Android Pulse' App Appearing on Everybody's Phones?
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson

            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.

            Credit: georgeclerk via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Android users started seeing a new "Android Pulse" app on their phones over the weekend. As it turns out, it's supposed to be there.
                                            Android Pulse is a Google-made app that works in the background to note any apps or processes that take up too many resources on your phone.
                                            The Play Store says the app is three days old, with over 10 million downloads, though APKMirror shows that Android Pulse has existed since March.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you keep tabs on your Android app updates in the Play Store, you might have noticed something odd: You have an app called "Android Pulse" on your phone. Most of us have way too many apps on our phones, and it's easy to forget that we downloaded some of them—especially when we install them once and never use them again. But I'd wager that not only do you have no recollection of downloading Android Pulse, but you have no idea what Android Pulse even is. I had certainly never heard of Android Pulse before Monday morning, though I admit I spend far more time on iOS than on Android. Luckily, I don't think any level of Android knowledge or use would prime one to know about the app, as it appears Android Pulse is only three days old. As reported by 9to5Google, Android Pulse started appearing in Play Store updates as early as Saturday morning. In fact, its Play Store listing shows that it was released on August 21 of this year by none other than Google itself. And yet, after only three days on the Play Store, Android Pulse has over 10 million downloads.    Android Pulse has been working in the background on your phoneAs it turns out, Google didn't silently install a random app on tens of millions of Android users' devices. Rather, it's the Play Store listing itself that's new, not Android Pulse. According to its Play Store description, Android Pulse "facilitates rule distribution for anomaly detection in critical system resource consumption by the Android operating system and installed applications." 
In layman's terms? Android Pulse keeps a virtual eye out for any suspicious processes that consume excessive system resources in both Android and your phone's apps. There are many possibilities there: It may be that Android Pulse looks for apps that put an unnecessary strain on the CPU or GPU, or system processes that drain your battery more than usual. Whatever the case, Android Pulse monitors for unusual activity affecting your phone and how it functions. And despite its new "app," there isn't much you can do with it. It isn't even clear if Android Pulse helps Android OS fix itself, or if Google simply receives the reports to help with future stability updates.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Interestingly, while the Play Store says the app is three days old, APKMirror says its first iteration dropped in March. Whatever the case, Android Pulse only made itself known this weekend, so it's news to most—if not all—of us. What should I do about Android Pulse?The short answer? Nothing. Android Pulse appears to be a background system resource that just so happens to appear in app form. In fact, based on screenshots from Android Authority, it doesn't even appear that you can uninstall it. You might be able to disable or force stop Pulse, but I'm not sure you'd want to. The "app" is designed to root out system hogs; I suspect it won't become one itself.

title: These Google Maps and Apple Maps Alternatives Still Call It ‘Lake Ontario’ (for Now)
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 2, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Jim WATSON / AFP via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Following Trump's executive order, Google Maps and Apple Maps have renamed Lake Ontario "Lake America."
                                            Google says it follows the U.S. Geographic Names Information System, and has updated its map accordingly.
                                            Trump directly appealed to Apple, on the other hand, to change the name on its map.
                                            Some other navigation apps have not changed Lake Ontario's name—at least, not yet.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Last week, U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario to "Lake America." The move was retaliation against Canada for walking away from contentious trade talks and in spite of the fact that Lake Ontario's name has nothing to do with the Canadian province. Regardless, tech companies are now dealing with the consequences.Why did Google Maps change Lake Ontario's name?If you live in the U.S., you may have opened Google Maps this past weekend to see that the app had already changed Lake Ontario's name. Even if you don't live in the U.S., you may see the name change: As it happens, there are now three different naming schemes for the lake in Google's navigation app. If you use the app in the U.S., you'll see "Lake America." If you use it in Canada, you'll see "Lake Ontario." If you use it anywhere else in the world, you'll see "Lake Ontario (Lake America)." Thanks, Google.
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Google
                    
    
Google did the same when Trump "changed" the name of the Gulf of Mexico to "Gulf of America." While Google explains in a blog post that its policy is to follow the naming conventions of the U.S. Geographic Names Information System, it's also arguable that the company doesn't want to get into hot water with the Trump Administration, lest it be punished with future policies that could hurt its trillion-dollar business. Now, Apple Maps is in the same boat. While Apple's app kept "Lake Ontario" on its map longer than Google, it has since changed the name as well. Trump reportedly urged Apple directly to make the switch. (Like Google, the company previously changed the Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America as well.) 
Whether you consider it basic bureaucratic compliance or corporate cowardice, Google Maps and Apple Maps now call the lake by its "new" name. It doesn't affect how the apps work (maybe unless you're looking for directions to, or information about, Lake Ontario), but if the change rankles you, you have other options: As it stands, there are now two key alternatives that still label it "Lake Ontario."As of this writing, only a couple of apps available to download call Lake Ontario by its official/"former" name. Whether that will remain true as the week goes on remains a question, but for now, the following apps are still reflecting the global consensus:
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
MapQuestOrganic MapsTechnically, Waze also still calls it Lake Ontario on its map, and the name pops up when you start to search for it. But once you tap the result, the app then swaps the name to Lake America. That's to be expected, given Google owns Waze, but the app initially tricked me into thinking it had maintained the previous status quo.Will other apps change Lake Ontario's name?Will these apps maintain the Lake Ontario name over the long term? When I first published this article, Apple hadn't changed the name, but I had expected them to. As I said above, Apple ultimately changed the Gulf of Mexico's name, so it followed that it would likely do the same with the lake. However, MapQuest and Organic Maps still call the Gulf of Mexico by its correct name, so chances are good they'll keep Lake Ontario on their maps for the foreseeable future.

                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple just announced a new keynote, where the company is expected to announce the latest iPhones.
                                            Leaks and rumors suggest Apple will reveal the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, which should offer small upgrades over the iPhone 17 Pro.
                                            The star of the show will be the iPhone Ultra, Apple's first foldable iPhone (and likely the company's most expensive iPhone to date).
                                            The keynote starts at 10 a.m. PT on Wednesday, Sept. 9.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        You don't need to follow leaks and rumors to know that Apple will announce the iPhone 18 next month. The company has revealed new iPhones once a year every year since its first smartphone launch back in 2007. The real unknown, of course, is what day exactly Apple will make these announcements. As of Wednesday, we know for sure. Ahead of the event, make sure to enter Lifehacker's Big Guessing Game. The quiz is now in its third round, and each correct guess gets you the chance to win the latest Apple Watch.Apple just announced its next big iPhone eventApple has set an official time and date for its iPhone 18 announcement. The company is scheduled to kick off its keynote on Wednesday, Sept. 9 at 10 a.m. PT. While Apple is inviting some media members to attend in person, anyone can watch the presentation live online. Apple's senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing, Greg Joswiak, confirmed the keynote in a post on X:

    
        This Tweet is currently unavailable. It might be loading or has been removed.
    

What will Apple announce at its iPhone event?We don't know for sure what Apple will reveal on Sept. 9, but leaks and rumors give us some good guesses. The math tells us that Apple will go from the iPhone 17 to the iPhone 18 this year, while the leaks suggest that we'll see the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the foldable "iPhone Ultra."(Apple may delay the standard iPhone 18 to 2027, per rumors.) 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max will likely be standard upgrades from the iPhone 17 Pro series: Expect better cameras, bigger batteries, new colors (including the new "light blue" and "dark cherry"), the new A20 chip, and higher price tags. The star of the show will be Apple's first foldable iPhone, which will come with many of the same internals as the iPhone 18 Pros, but may ship with Touch ID instead of Face ID, and, of course, with two display types: a smaller outer display, which opens up to reveal a larger inner display. This might be Apple's most expensive iPhone yet, fetching over $2,000, but we'll have to wait and see once Apple officially announces its price tag.

title: Google Will Soon Let You Tell It What Stories You Want to See in Your Discovery Feed
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 21, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: John Lamb via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Google will soon let you tell its app what stories you want to see in your Discovery feed, adding another natual language prompt to the experience.
                                            Once the feature rolls out, you can tap the three-dot menu on any story to tell Gemini what topics you're looking for, and continue refining as you wish.
                                            In addition, you can customize your audio briefings in Google News, and you'll likely see Google's "Add as preferred source" button on more websites.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        I don't know what the far future of tech looks like, but I know what's in store for the near future: AI. Specifically, AI that responds to natural language prompts. It's already the reality for many platforms, apps, and services: Rather than doing things yourself, you tell the AI what you want done, and it follows suit. Natural language commands are popping up everywhere, from coding platforms to playlist generators. Now, apparently, they're coming to your news app too. Natural language commands are coming to the Google app's Discovery feed
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Google
                    
    
Google announced a handful of changes coming to its self-named app on Friday. Perhaps most notably among the developments is the new ability to "tune" and "tailor" your Discovery feed to your liking—not by giving feedback for specific articles or sources, but by simply telling Google what news you want to see, and what you don't. Here's how it works, according to Google: Once the feature is live in your Google app, you can tap any three-dot menu in the feed to tell Google how you want to change your feed. When you do, you'll pull up a new window that reads "What do you want to see." Here, you'll find sample prompts ("Show me content from...," I want videos about..." etc.) and a text field to enter them in. As an example, Google says you can enter a query like "show me kitchen renovation tips and ideas." Gemini will then show you a list of the types of stories it thinks you'll want to see (e.g., "Modern layout ideas and floor plans," "Budget-friendly cabinet and countertop refreshes," etc.). If that looks good, you can hit "Refresh your feed."
If you aren't happy with Gemini's first interpretation of your instruction, you can refine it before refreshing your feed. You can send another prompt (e.g., "can you focus on eco-friendly and sustainable upgrades?") and see how Gemini responds. You can repeat this process until you're happy with the direction Gemini is taking, then hit "Refresh your feed" to see what it came up with. (Of course, you can tap a three-dot menu again to continue changing the experience.) Google says these updates will roll out "in the coming days."
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Other changes coming to the Google appIn addition to this natural language feature, Google also announced two new changes for its app. First, Google is making it easier to customize the audio briefings you might receive in Google News on Android. Now, you'll be able to choose specific topics you want to hear, including between main topics and subtopics. For example, you could say you want to hear science and technology news, but only about neuroscience and space, not environment, gaming, or virtual reality. There are a lot of curation possibilities here. In addition, Google says it's rolling out a new "Preferred Sources" button for publishers to use. You may have seen the first iteration of this button on Lifehacker articles. While it isn't clear what's new with the latest version, this button lets you tell Google that you want to see more articles from a particular publisher for topics going forward. If you add Lifehacker as a preferred source, for example, you may see our articles for topics like AI, Apple, and security when they appear in your feed.

schema.headline: Google Will Soon Let You Tell It What Stories You Want to See in Your Discovery Feed
